LA:025.statement: Define $P:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by $P(x,y,z)=(x,y,0)$. Prove that $P$ is linear and idempotent. Then prove that every $v\in\mathbb R^3$ has a unique decomposition $v=r+k$ satisfying $P(r)=r$ and $P(k)=0$, and identify the two summands as $r=P(v)$ and $k=v-P(v)$.
permittedResults: Linearity can be checked by additivity and compatibility with scalar multiplication.
For an idempotent map, applying $P$ to a fixed-plus-kernel decomposition isolates the fixed summand.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Verify additivity, homogeneity, and $P(P(v))=P(v)$ coordinatewise. Next: Try $r=P(v)$ and $k=v-P(v)$, then apply $P$ to both pieces. Finally: For uniqueness, apply $P$ to $v=r+k$ and use $P(r)=r$ and $P(k)=0$.

milestones.criterion: Checks both linearity identities and idempotence.
Constructs $P(v)$ and $v-P(v)$ and verifies the fixed/kernel conditions.
Proves uniqueness by applying $P$ to an arbitrary competing decomposition.

commonErrors.description: Claims idempotence means $P(v)=v$ for every vector.
commonErrors.consequence: Idempotence is $P(P(v))=P(v)$; vectors with nonzero third coordinate are not fixed.

commonErrors.description: Uses $k=P(v)-v$ as the kernel summand in $v=r+k$.
commonErrors.consequence: That sign gives $r+k=2P(v)-v$; the correct kernel term is $v-P(v)$.

hintTree.content: Verify additivity, homogeneity, and $P(P(v))=P(v)$ coordinatewise.
Try $r=P(v)$ and $k=v-P(v)$, then apply $P$ to both pieces.
For uniqueness, apply $P$ to $v=r+k$ and use $P(r)=r$ and $P(k)=0$.

LA:025.canonicalSolution:
Coordinate calculations give $P(u+v)=P(u)+P(v)$ and $P(cu)=cP(u)$, so $P$ is linear; also $P(P(x,y,z))=P(x,y,0)=(x,y,0)=P(x,y,z)$. Set $r=P(v)$ and $k=v-P(v)$. Idempotence gives $P(r)=r$, while linearity and idempotence give $P(k)=P(v)-P(P(v))=0$, and $v=r+k$. If $v=r'+k'$ with $P(r')=r'$ and $P(k')=0$, applying $P$ gives $P(v)=r'$. Thus $r'=P(v)$ and then $k'=v-P(v)$, proving uniqueness.

LA:026.objective: Solve the scalar constraints behind projection-like diagonal maps and identify every case.
LA:026.statement: For $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$, define $T_{\lambda,\mu}(x,y)=(\lambda x,\mu y)$. Prove $T_{\lambda,\mu}^2=T_{\lambda,\mu}$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\in\{0,1\}$. Two linear maps are equal when their values agree on every vector.

Proves the converse for all vectors.

commonErrors.consequence: A multiplier such as $2$ produces $T^2(x,y)$ with coefficient $4$, so the scalar equations are necessary.

commonErrors.consequence: The second coordinate is independent and requires a separate test of $\mu$.

The two coordinates give $\lambda^2=\lambda$ and $\mu^2=\mu$.

LA:027.title: All decompositions through two coordinate planes
LA:027.objective: Compute an intersection and classify a one-parameter family of nonunique decompositions.
LA:027.statement:
In $\mathbb R^3$, let $U=\{(x,y,0):x,y\in\mathbb R\}$ and $W=\{(0,y,z):y,z\in\mathbb R\}$. Prove $U\cap W=\{(0,t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}$. Then prove that every decomposition of $(a,b,c)$ as $u+w$ with $u\in U$ and $w\in W$ has the unique form
  $$(a,b,c)=(a,t,0)+(0,b-t,c)$$
  for one real parameter $t$, and verify that every $t$ gives a valid decomposition.
permittedResults: Membership in each coordinate plane is encoded by one zero coordinate.
Equality of triples can be compared coordinatewise.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: A vector in both planes must have first and third coordinates zero. Next: In a decomposition, the first coordinate of $u$ and third coordinate of $w$ are forced. Finally: Let $t$ be the second coordinate of $u$ and solve for the second coordinate of $w$.

milestones.criterion: Computes the intersection by enforcing both plane conditions.
Derives all forced coordinates and the one free parameter in an arbitrary decomposition.
Proves both uniqueness of the parameter for a given decomposition and validity for every parameter value.

commonErrors.description: Claims the decomposition is unique because the two planes are different.
commonErrors.consequence: Their intersection is the entire $y$-axis, which produces a one-parameter family of decompositions.

commonErrors.description: Uses $(a,t,0)+(0,b+t,c)$ as the family.
commonErrors.consequence: The second coordinates then add to $b+2t$ rather than $b$.

hintTree.content: A vector in both planes must have first and third coordinates zero.
In a decomposition, the first coordinate of $u$ and third coordinate of $w$ are forced.
Let $t$ be the second coordinate of $u$ and solve for the second coordinate of $w$.

LA:027.canonicalSolution:
A vector in $U\cap W$ has the form $(x,y,0)$ and also $(0,s,z)$, so coordinate comparison forces $x=0$, $z=0$, and leaves one free value $t=y=s$. Thus the intersection is the $y$-axis. If $(a,b,c)=u+w$ with $u=(x,t,0)\in U$ and $w=(0,s,z)\in W$, comparing coordinates gives $x=a$, $z=c$, and $t+s=b$, hence $s=b-t$. Therefore every decomposition has the displayed form, with $t$ uniquely equal to the second coordinate of $u$. Conversely, for every real $t$, the two displayed summands lie in $U$ and $W$ and add to $(a,b,c)$.

LA:028.title: When a line complements the coordinate plane
LA:028.objective: Prove a sharp plane-line complement criterion and compute every component.

Let $H=\{(x,y,0):x,y\in\mathbb R\}$ and let $L=\operatorname{span}(a,b,c)$ in $\mathbb R^3$. Prove $\mathbb R^3=H\oplus L$ if and only if $c
e0$. When $c
e0$, compute the unique decomposition of $(x,y,z)$. When $c=0$, prove $(0,0,1)
otin H+L$.

A direct-sum decomposition is equivalent to existence and uniqueness of the two summands.

Constructs and verifies the plane component and proves uniqueness.
Uses $(0,0,1)$ to prove failure of spanning when $c=0$.

commonErrors.description: Claims every nonzero vector spans a complement to the coordinate plane.
commonErrors.consequence: A nonzero vector with $c=0$ lies inside the plane and cannot supply the missing third-coordinate direction.

commonErrors.description: Uses $t=z$ rather than $t=z/c$.
commonErrors.consequence: The third coordinate of $t(a,b,c)$ is $tc$, so division by the nonzero $c$ is required.

Assume $c\ne0$. In any decomposition $(x,y,z)=(r,s,0)+t(a,b,c)$, the third coordinate gives $t=z/c$. The first two then force $r=x-az/c$ and $s=y-bz/c$. These values yield

LA:029.objective: Construct the canonical matrix splitting and prove that no competing splitting exists.
LA:029.statement: For a real $2\times2$ matrix $A$, prove there is a unique decomposition $A=S+K$ with $S^T=S$ and $K^T=-K$. Compute $S=(A+A^T)/2$ and $K=(A-A^T)/2$, and prove the symmetric and skew-symmetric subspaces intersect only at $0$.

Matrix equality and transpose identities may be checked entrywise.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Construct the two candidates by adding and subtracting the transpose. Next: For uniqueness, write $K=A-S$ and impose both symmetry of $S$ and skew-symmetry of $A-S$. Finally: A matrix that is both symmetric and skew-symmetric equals its own negative, so every entry vanishes.

Proves a matrix in both subspaces must be zero.
Uses the zero intersection to establish uniqueness of the decomposition.

commonErrors.consequence: Then the proposed summands add to $2A$ rather than $A$.

Set $S=(A+A^T)/2$ and $K=(A-A^T)/2$. Entrywise addition gives $S+K=A$, while transposing yields $S^T=S$ and $K^T=-K$. If $A=S_1+K_1$ is another such decomposition, then $S-S_1=K_1-K$. Thus $S=S_1$ and $K=K_1$. The same argument with a matrix already in both subspaces proves their intersection is $\{0\}$.

LA:045.canonicalSolution:
For a fixed $A$, the displayed formula gives a horizontal vector plus a graph vector. In any such decomposition, the second coordinate forces the graph parameter to be $w$, and the first then forces the horizontal part to be $u-Aw$, proving uniqueness. Conversely, fix a complement $C$. Decomposing $(0,w)$ shows that some $(u,w)$ lies in $C$. If both $(u,w)$ and $(v,w)$ lie in $C$, then $(-u,0)+(u,w)$ and $(-v,0)+(v,w)$ are two decompositions of $(0,w)$, so $u=v$. Define $Aw$ to be this unique $u$. Because $C$ is closed under sums and scalar multiples, both $(Ax+Ay,x+y)$ and $(cAx,cx)$ lie in $C$; uniqueness over the second coordinate gives $A(x+y)=Ax+Ay$ and $A(cx)=cAx$. Thus $A$ is linear. A pair $(u,w)$ lies in $C$ exactly when uniqueness gives $u=Aw$, so $C=G_A$. Any other linear map with graph $C$ has the same value above each $w$, proving uniqueness.

    B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
    C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

A family is a basis when every target has a unique coefficient expansion.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Compare the off-diagonal entry first to determine $\gamma$. Next: Use the two diagonal entries after substituting that value. Finally: For uniqueness, repeat the entry comparison for an arbitrary competing triple.

commonErrors.consequence: Because $C$ also contributes to both diagonal entries, the diagonal coefficients must be adjusted by subtracting $q$.

commonErrors.description: Checks that the proposed expansion works but does not prove uniqueness.
commonErrors.consequence: A basis-coordinate claim requires showing every competing coefficient triple is forced.

Use the two diagonal entries after substituting that value.
For uniqueness, repeat the entry comparison for an arbitrary competing triple.

LA:074.title: The dimension formula for a subspace sum
LA:074.objective: Prove the Grassmann dimension identity from compatible bases.
LA:074.statement:
Let $U$ and $W$ be finite-dimensional subspaces of a vector space over a field $K$. Prove
  $$\dim(U+W)+\dim(U\cap W)=\dim U+\dim W.$$

The cardinality of a finite basis equals the dimension.

Finally: To prove independence, separate a zero relation into a vector of $U$ equal to a vector of $W$, then use the intersection basis.

Proves both spanning and independence of the combined family.

commonErrors.consequence: Vectors representing the shared intersection can create duplicate directions; the bases must be coordinated through $U\cap W$.

commonErrors.description: States $\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W$ without subtracting overlap.
commonErrors.consequence: The intersection directions are counted in both dimensions and must be corrected once.

Show $B_0\cup B_U\cup B_W$ spans $U+W$.

Choose a basis $B_0$ of $U\cap W$. Extend it to a basis $B_0\cup B_U$ of $U$ and independently to a basis $B_0\cup B_W$ of $W$. Every $u+w\in U+W$ expands using $B_0\cup B_U\cup B_W$, so that union spans the sum. In a zero relation among the union, move the $B_U$ part to one side and the $B_W$ part to the other. Their common value lies in both $U$ and $W$, hence in $U\cap W$ and therefore is a combination of $B_0$. Independence of the two extended bases then forces all coefficients to vanish. Thus the union is a basis of $U+W$. Counting gives $\dim(U+W)=|B_0|+|B_U|+|B_W|$, while $\dim U=|B_0|+|B_U|$, $\dim W=|B_0|+|B_W|$, and $\dim(U\cap W)=|B_0|$; rearrangement proves the formula.
